description.title: Model organism or animal sample from Trichinella nativa

assembly_info.comments:
Trichinella nativa is one of two major species/genotypes of Trichinella that are resistant to freezing and that populate the Holarctic above the -60C isotherm. It is a zoonotic parasite found predominantly in carnivores and unlike Trichinella spiralis, infects swine poorly to not at all. The isolate used to obtain this data was assigned the accession number ISS45 by the International Trichinella Reference Center (ITRC) and was obtained from a Canadian artic fox (Alopex lagopusin) in 1980 by T. Dick (J Wildl Dis. 18:169-73;1982). All pertinent information on the isolate can be obtained from the ITRC website (http://www.iss.it/site/trichinella/scripts/sear.asp). The isolate has been passaged in Swiss Webster mice approximately 1.5X/year since 1986. Genomic and Transcriptomic DNA were isolated by Dr. Dante Zarlenga and Sonstegard, T. and confirmed to be T. nativa by PCR.

Genomic Illumina paired end reads from three collections of Trichinella nativa data were mapped against the Trichinella spiralis reference (ABIR00000000) using the bwa aligner (release 0.6.1-r104) with default parameters. T. nativa genomic DNA that had been stored at -20C, room temperature and 50C (6,203,601, 24,292,866 and 50,521,379 pairs respectively) were used as queries against the T. spiralis genome sequence of length 64,330,921bp. When combined these three data sets covered 82.1% of the reference to a depth of approximately 126.6x. Samtools mpileup was then run using the combined, coordinate sorted bam file, and the T.spiralis genomic reference. The arguments used with mpileup were "-d100000 -C50 -B -I", and the vcfutils.pl varFilter was called applying a more stringent maximum, useable depth of -D252 (based on a suggestion to use approximately 2x the observed, average depth (126.6x)). This process identified 1,053,763 snps across the T. spiralis backbone. We then subtracted the T. spiralis reference from the results by omitting all snp loci where AF1=1 in the vcf ('AF1' is the 'alternate allele frequency' value). After removing the T. spiralis variant loci, our merged dataset was left with 169,259 snp loci within T. nativa. We then used GATK's FastaAlternateReferenceMaker method (http://www.broadinstitute.org/gatk/gatkdocs/org_broadinstitute_gatk_tools_walkers_fasta_FastaAlternateReferenceMaker.html) and a bed file comprising only regions where T. nativa data overlapped the T. spiralis backbone to construct a T. nativa consensus populated with the T. nativa allele at each detected snp loci. In addition, Reads that did not map to the T. spiralis reference were assembled using Velvet, utilizing the VelvetOptimizer (http://bioinformatics.net.au/software.velvetoptimiser.shtml), which selected the kmer size of 39 for the optmimum assembly. The number of large contigs (Lcon) and N50 were further used to improve the assembly. Blat was then used to compare the assembled contigs to the contigs created by alignment to the T. spiralis genomic reference and all contigs greater than 500 bp, with 50% coverage and 80% identity, were retained in the assembly.

The repeat library was generated using Repeatmodeler (A.F.A. Smit, R. Hubley & P. Green http://repeatmasker.org). The Ribosomal RNA genes were identified using RNAmmer (Lagesen et. al., 2007 Nucleic Acids Res.) and transfer RNA's were identified with tRNAscan-SE (Lowe and Eddy, Nucleic Acids Res. 1997). Non-coding RNAs, such as microRNAs, were identified by sequence homology search of the Rfam database (Griffiths-Jones et. al., 2003 Nucleic Acids Res.). Repeats and predicted RNA's were then masked using RepeatMasker (A. Smit, R. Hubley & P. Green http://repeatmasker.org). Protein-coding genes were predicted using a combination of ab initio programs Snap (Korf, 2004 BCM Bioinformatics), Fgenesh (Salamov A., Solovyev V. 2000, Genome Res.) and Augustus (M. Stanke, et. al., 2008 Bioinformatics) and the annotation pipeline tool Maker (M. Yandell et. al., 2007 Genomc Research) which aligns mRNA, EST and protein information from same species or cross-species to aid in gene structure determination and modifications. A c onsensus gene set from the above prediction algorithms was generated, using a logical, hierarchical approach developed at the Genome institute. Gene product naming was determined by BER (http://ber.sourceforge.net).

For information regarding this assembly or project, or any other GSC genome project, please visit our Genome Groups web page (http://genome.wustl.edu/genome_group_index.cgi) and email the designated contact person. For specific questions regarding the T. nativa genome project contact Makedonka Mitreva (mmitreva@genome.wustl.edu) at Washington University School of Medicine. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) provided funds for this project.
